citation: Shiping Cheng. Haplotype-resolved genome assembly and allele-specific gene expression in cultivated ginger. Horticulture Research. 2021.
summary: A haplotype-resolved, chromosome-scale genome of cultivated diploid ginger, anchored to 11 pairs of pseudochromosomes, with an analysis of how the two alleles of each gene are expressed.

citation: Eliana L. Peña, Sunyoung Kang, François Gaascht, Claudia Schmidt‐Dannert. Identification of Type III Polyketide Synthases from Ginger for Dehydrogingerdione and Curcumin Biosynthesis by Engineered Escherichia coli. ACS Synthetic Biology. 2026.
summary: Biochemical identification of type III polyketide synthases from ginger and turmeric, including a ginger enzyme (ZoPKS2) that makes 6-dehydrogingerdione, the first enzyme shown to build the gingerol-type skeleton.

citation: Connell DW, Sutherland MD. A re-examination of gingerol, shogaol, and zingerone, the pungent principles of ginger ( Zingiber officinale Roscoe). Australian Journal of Chemistry. 1969.
summary: Connell and Sutherland re-examined the acetone extract of dried ginger rhizome and characterised its pungent principles. They established the gingerols as a homologous series of hydroxy ketones with side chains of different lengths, and showed that shogaols and zingerone arise from them rather than being primary constituents of the fresh plant. The paper set the chemical vocabulary that later work on ginger's pungency still uses.
why_it_mattered: It fixed which compounds make ginger hot and established that shogaols and zingerone are largely products of processing, the basis for every later study of how drying and cooking change ginger.

citation: Stuart GA. Chinese Materia Medica: Vegetable Kingdom, 'Zingiber officinale', pp. 465–466. Shanghai: American Presbyterian Mission Press. 1911.
summary: George Arthur Stuart's Chinese Materia Medica, a revision of an earlier work by Porter Smith, summarises the Chinese pharmacopoeia for Western readers. Its ginger entry distinguishes fresh and dried ginger and their uses, notes the regional sources of the best ginger and records the preference for southern Chinese ginger in preserves. The book is in the public domain and was read from a scan.

citation: Megan Crichton. Orally consumed ginger and human health: an umbrella review. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2022.
summary: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of oral ginger, grading the certainty of evidence for each health outcome; the strongest support was for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and some metabolic and inflammatory markers.

citation: Heitmann K et al. Safety of ginger use in pregnancy: results from a large population-based cohort study. European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2012.
summary: Heitmann and colleagues used the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort, 68,522 women of whom 1,020 reported taking ginger, to compare those exposed to ginger in pregnancy with those not exposed. Ginger use was not associated with a higher risk of congenital malformations, stillbirth or perinatal death, preterm birth, low birthweight or low Apgar scores. It is the largest study of ginger safety in pregnancy and is cited by the European regulator.

citation: European Medicines Agency, Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products. European Union herbal monograph on Zingiber officinale Roscoe, rhizoma. Final, Revision 1 (EMA/HMPC/885789/2022). European Medicines Agency. 2025.
summary: The European Medicines Agency's revised herbal monograph on ginger rhizome, which accepts well-established use only for motion sickness in adults, lists traditional uses, and sets out contraindications, warnings and pregnancy advice.

citation: Suzanna Maria Zick. Pharmacokinetics of 6-Gingerol, 8-Gingerol, 10-Gingerol, and 6-Shogaol and Conjugate Metabolites in Healthy Human Subjects. Cancer Epidemiology Biomarkers & Prevention. 2008.
summary: Zick and colleagues gave single oral doses of ginger extract to healthy volunteers and measured 6-, 8- and 10-gingerol and 6-shogaol in blood. The free compounds were barely detectable; almost all circulated as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates, which peaked within about an hour and were cleared within a few hours. The study defines the bioavailability problem for ginger in humans.
why_it_mattered: It was the first human pharmacokinetic study of the main ginger phenolics and showed how little free compound reaches the blood.

citation: Yule H, Burnell AC. Hobson-Jobson: a glossary of colloquial Anglo-Indian words and phrases, new ed. by W. Crooke, s.v. 'Ginger', pp. 374–375. London: John Murray. 1903.
summary: Hobson-Jobson, Yule and Burnell's glossary of Anglo-Indian words, revised by William Crooke in 1903, traces the history of words that passed between Indian languages and English. Its entry on ginger follows the word from Sanskrit and Prakrit through Greek, Latin and Arabic into English, with dated quotations. The book is in the public domain and was read from a scan.

Volume 1 (Sūtrasthāna) sets out groups of drugs, among them the trikaṭu group of long pepper, black pepper and ginger (śṛṅgavera), with the conditions each group was held to treat. summary: Flückiger and Hanbury's Pharmacographia, in its second edition, is a history of the principal plant drugs in British and American commerce. The ginger entry covers names, botany, cultivation regions, preparation of the dried rhizome (scraped and unscraped), commerce and the earliest documentary references. It is in the public domain and was read from a scan.

citation: Aram B. Caribbean ginger and Atlantic trade, 1570–1648. Journal of Global History 10(3). 2015.
summary: Aram traced the rise of ginger as a cash crop in the Spanish and Portuguese Caribbean between 1570 and 1648 and its place in Atlantic trade. He argues that preferences for ginger in northern and southern Europe differed in ways shaped by humoral medicine. The study connects the colonial plantation economy with the European medical demand for spices.

citation: Morgan JP, Tulloss TC. The Jake Walk Blues: A Toxicologic Tragedy Mirrored in American Popular Music. Annals of Internal Medicine. 1976.
summary: Morgan and Tulloss retold the 1930 epidemic of paralysis in the United States caused by an adulterated Jamaica ginger extract, known as 'jake'. The extract was drunk to evade Prohibition, and thousands of people were paralysed by a toxic adulterant later identified as an organophosphate. The paper traces how the epidemic was recorded in blues songs of the time.
why_it_mattered: It is the best-known account of the jake leg epidemic and links the toxicology to the cultural record.

citation: W. John Kress. The phylogeny and a new classification of the gingers (Zingiberaceae): evidence from molecular data. American Journal of Botany. 2002.
summary: Kress and colleagues built a molecular phylogeny of the ginger family from nuclear and plastid DNA sequences. The analysis did not support the traditional four tribes and led them to propose a new classification into four subfamilies and several tribes. It is the standard framework for relationships within the Zingiberaceae.
why_it_mattered: It replaced the nineteenth-century classification of the ginger family with one based on DNA and is the basis for later family-level work.

citation: Dongzhu Jiang. Complete chloroplast genomes provide insights into evolution and phylogeny of Zingiber (Zingiberaceae). BMC Genomics. 2023.
summary: Comparative analysis of complete chloroplast genomes from Zingiber species, giving a genus-level phylogeny and candidate DNA markers for telling species apart.

citation: Hong‐Lei Li. Haplotype-resolved genome of diploid ginger (Zingiber officinale) and its unique gingerol biosynthetic pathway. Horticulture Research. 2021.
summary: A haplotype-resolved genome of the ginger cultivar 'Zhugen', with transcriptome and metabolome data used to propose a backbone pathway of twelve enzyme families for gingerol biosynthesis.

citation: Hans Wohlmuth. Gingerol Content of Diploid and Tetraploid Clones of Ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe). Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry. 2005.
summary: Wohlmuth and colleagues measured gingerols and shogaols in fresh rhizomes of 17 ginger clones grown in Australia, including diploid cultivars and tetraploid lines. Gingerol content varied widely between clones, and the tetraploids did not have more than their diploid parents. The paper also established that fresh ginger contains little shogaol, which forms on drying and heating.

citation: Ma X, Gang DR. Metabolic profiling of in vitro micropropagated and conventionally greenhouse grown ginger (Zingiber officinale). Phytochemistry. 2006.
summary: Ma and Gang compared the metabolite profiles of ginger plants micropropagated in tissue culture with plants grown conventionally in a greenhouse. The profiles were broadly similar, so micropropagation did not compromise the plants' chemistry. Because ginger is propagated clonally and carries disease from one generation to the next, the result supports clean planting stock.
why_it_mattered: It showed that clean, tissue-cultured ginger keeps the chemistry of conventionally grown plants, a practical result for growing ginger under glass.

citation: Raghavan Ramakrishnan Nair. Variation in pollen fertility and chromosome number among germplasm collections of ginger (Zingiber officinaleRosc.). Caryologia. 2016.
summary: Ramakrishnan Nair and colleagues measured pollen fertility in 21 germplasm collections of ginger by staining and by in vitro germination. Fertility varied widely between collections, and some showed much higher fertility than expected for a crop usually described as sterile. The study suggests that sexual breeding of ginger may be possible in some lines.

citation: Ramachandran K. Chromosome Numbers in Zingiberaceae. CYTOLOGIA. 1969.
summary: Ramachandran counted chromosomes in 27 species from 11 genera of the ginger family, several for the first time. The counts established base numbers for the genera and placed Zingiber in the cytological context of its family. It remains a reference for the chromosome number of ginger.
why_it_mattered: It is the classic cytological survey of the ginger family, cited for the chromosome number of Zingiber officinale.

citation: Shan Liang, Mingli Hu, Hao-chuan Lin, Hanjun He. Transcriptional regulations of pollen tube reception are associated with the fertility of the ginger species Zingiber zerumbet and Zingiber corallinum. Frontiers in Plant Science. 2023.
summary: A comparison of a sexually fertile and a largely clonal Zingiber species, locating the failure of sexual reproduction at pollen-tube reception and linking it to differences in gene expression.

citation: Adaniya S, Shoda M, Fujieda K. Effects of Day Length on Flowering and Rhizome Swelling in Ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe). Journal of the Japanese Society for Horticultural Science. 1989.
summary: Adaniya and colleagues grew three Japanese ginger cultivars under day lengths from 10 to 16 hours. Long days favoured leafy growth and flowering, while short days suppressed shoot growth and promoted swelling of the rhizome. The experiment shows that rhizome formation in ginger responds to photoperiod, which matters for growing it out of season or under glass.
why_it_mattered: It is the classic experimental demonstration that day length controls the switch from shoot growth to rhizome swelling in ginger.

citation: Huanfang Liu, Chelsea Dvorak Specht, Tong Zhao, Jingping Liao. Morphological Anatomy of Leaf and Rhizome in Zingiber officinale Roscoe, with Emphasis on Secretory Structures. HortScience. 2020.
summary: Liu and colleagues studied the anatomy of ginger leaf and rhizome at several stages of development with light and electron microscopy. They described the secretory cells in which the oil and resin are made and stored, and how these cells develop. The paper explains where in the plant the compounds of interest are made.

citation: Josie C. Torrecampo, Neaven Bon Joy M. Marcial, Chuckcris P. Tenebro, Janine J. Salcepuedes. Spatial Profiling of Gingerol and Shogaol Analogues in Intact Zingiber officinale Rhizomes Using MALDI Mass Spectrometry Imaging. Molecules. 2026.
summary: A mass-spectrometry imaging study (MALDI) that maps where gingerols and shogaols sit in intact ginger rhizome sections, showing their uneven spatial distribution.

citation: Zijing Chen. A genome assembly of ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe) provides insights into genome evolution and 6‐gingerol biosynthesis. The Plant Journal. 2024.
summary: A haplotype-resolved genome of the northern Chinese cultivar 'Small Laiwu Ginger', with evidence on genome evolution and the transcriptional regulation of 6-gingerol biosynthesis.

citation: Jiang H et al. Metabolic profiling and phylogenetic analysis of medicinal Zingiber species: Tools for authentication of ginger (Zingiber officinale Rosc.). Phytochemistry. 2005.
summary: Jiang and colleagues combined DNA phylogeny with metabolic profiling of ginger and related Zingiber species. Ginger accessions were genetically almost uniform but differed in their chemistry, and related species could be told apart by both. The study showed how chemistry and DNA can be used to authenticate ginger material.
why_it_mattered: It showed that cultivated ginger is genetically near-uniform while its chemistry varies, a key point for both quality control and the domestication question.

citation: Kizhakkayil J, Sasikumar B. Diversity, characterization and utilization of ginger: a review. Plant Genetic Resources. 2011.
summary: Kizhakkayil and Sasikumar reviewed the diversity of cultivated ginger and its characterisation and use. They place its origin in the Indo-Malayan region and its domestication in India and China, and describe the variation among cultivars despite the plant's sterility. The review is a standard reference for ginger germplasm.

citation: Watt G (ed.); Murray J. A Dictionary of the Economic Products of India, vol. 6 part 4, 'Zingiber officinale' (article by J. Murray), pp. 359–366. Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing. 1893.
summary: George Watt's Dictionary of the Economic Products of India was the government's reference work on Indian commodities. Its long ginger article, by J. Murray, gives the Indian names, cultivation and trade, quotes Linschoten's account of the trade in 1596, summarises Indian domestic medicine and reports J. C. Thresh's chemical analyses of commercial gingers. It is in the public domain and was read from a scan.

citation: Yuge Gao. Preparation, pungency and bioactivity of gingerols from ginger ( Zingiber officinale Roscoe): a review. Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition. 2022.
summary: A review of the preparation, pungency and reported bioactivities of gingerols, including extraction methods and the chemistry of their conversion to shogaols.

citation: Bhattarai S et al. The Stability of Gingerol and Shogaol in Aqueous Solutions. Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences. 2001.
summary: Bhattarai and colleagues measured how 6-gingerol and 6-shogaol degrade in water across a range of temperatures and acidities. Gingerol dehydrates to shogaol and the reaction is reversible; the rate depends on heat and on pH, and 6-gingerol was most stable near pH 4. The study gives kinetic grounds for why cooking and storage change the balance of ginger's pungent compounds.
why_it_mattered: It is the standard kinetic account of the gingerol–shogaol conversion in water, which this guide uses to explain what boiling, brewing and acidic recipes do to ginger.

citation: Hyun Jo Koo. Suites of Terpene Synthases Explain Differential Terpenoid Production in Ginger and Turmeric Tissues. PLoS ONE. 2012.
summary: Koo and colleagues identified and characterised a suite of terpene synthases from ginger and turmeric tissues. The enzymes and their products explained much of the difference in the essential oils of the two plants and of different tissues. The work linked the aroma of ginger to specific genes.

citation: Yoko Iijima, Takao Koeduka, Hideyuki Suzuki, Kikue Kubota. Biosynthesis of geranial, a potent aroma compound in ginger rhizome (Zingiber officinale): Molecular cloning and characterization of geraniol dehydrogenase. Plant Biotechnology. 2014.
summary: Iijima and colleagues investigated how geranial, the main citrus-scented aroma compound of fresh ginger, is made in the rhizome. They identified the enzymes that convert geraniol and its derivatives to geranial. The study explains part of the difference in aroma between fresh and dried ginger.

citation: John P. Bartley. Effects of drying on flavour compounds in Australian-grown ginger (Zingiber officinale). Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture. 2000.
summary: Bartley extracted the flavour compounds of fresh and dried Australian-grown ginger with supercritical carbon dioxide and compared them. Drying reduced gingerol content, increased terpene hydrocarbons and converted some aroma compounds into others. The study is one of the clearest early comparisons of how drying changes ginger's flavour chemistry.

citation: Ghulam Mustafa Kamal, Nafia Nazi, Asma Sabir, Muhammad Saqib. Yield and Chemical Composition of Ginger Essential Oils as Affected by Inter-Varietal Variation and Drying Treatments of Rhizome. Separations. 2023.
summary: A comparison of essential-oil yield and composition among ginger varieties and extraction methods.

citation: E. H. Thompson. GINGER RHIZOME: A NEW SOURCE OF PROTEOLYTIC ENZYME. Journal of Food Science. 1973.
summary: Thompson and colleagues characterised a protein-digesting enzyme extracted from ginger rhizome and tested it on serum albumin, collagen and muscle proteins. The enzyme, later named zingibain, broke down collagen and could tenderise meat. The paper is the first description of the ginger protease.
why_it_mattered: It identified the enzyme behind ginger's use as a meat tenderiser and in milk curd desserts.

citation: Xiaoning Huang, L.J. Chen, Y.B. Luo, H.Y. Guo. Purification, characterization, and milk coagulating properties of ginger proteases. Journal of Dairy Science. 2011.
summary: Huang and colleagues purified proteases from ginger and studied their properties, including the temperatures at which they are active. They showed that the enzymes coagulate milk, the basis of the Cantonese ginger milk curd. The study connects a traditional dish to enzyme chemistry.

citation: Schwertner HA, Rios DC. High-performance liquid chromatographic analysis of 6-gingerol, 8-gingerol, 10-gingerol, and 6-shogaol in ginger-containing dietary supplements, spices, teas, and beverages. Journal of Chromatography B. 2007.
summary: Schwertner and Rios developed a high-performance liquid chromatography method for 6-, 8- and 10-gingerol and 6-shogaol and applied it to ginger supplements, foods and beverages. Contents varied widely between products and many supplements did not match their label claims. The study shows why ginger products are hard to compare.
why_it_mattered: It established a widely used analytical method and documented how variable commercial ginger products are.

citation: Dymock W, Warden CJH, Hooper D. Pharmacographia Indica, vol. 3, 'Zingiber officinale', pp. 420–428. London: Kegan Paul; Bombay: Education Society's Press. 1893.
summary: The third volume of Pharmacographia Indica, by Dymock, Warden and Hooper, gives a long entry on ginger drawn from Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic sources and from colonial trade records. It records Indian names, classical uses, domestic remedies such as fresh juice with honey for cough, the Chinese method of preserving ginger and trade figures for the late nineteenth century. The volume is in the public domain and was read from a scan.

summary: Nam examined three medieval European pharmacology texts to explain why Asian spices such as pepper, ginger and cinnamon were valued as medicines. In humoral theory their 'hot' and 'dry' qualities fitted them to treat cold, wet conditions, and their rarity added to their prestige. The article frames the medieval medical use of ginger.

summary: Harry Marshall Ward studied the 'ginger-beer plant', the gelatinous starter used to brew home ginger beer, and showed that it is not a single organism. He identified it as a partnership of a yeast and a bacterium living together, each contributing to the fermentation. The paper is an early classic of microbial symbiosis and was read from a scan.

citation: John P. Morgan. Jamaica Ginger Paralysis: Forty-seven-Year Follow-up. Archives of Neurology. 1978.
summary: Morgan and colleagues examined survivors of the 1930 Jamaica ginger poisoning 47 years later. The adulterant, triorthocresyl phosphate, was first thought to damage only peripheral nerves, but the 11 survivors interviewed in eastern Tennessee showed the spasticity and abnormal reflexes of an upper motor neuron syndrome. The lesions lay in the spinal cord, and the study clarified the long-term neurology of the epidemic.

citation: John P. Morgan. The Jamaica Ginger Paralysis. JAMA. 1982.
summary: Morgan's review of the Jamaica ginger paralysis describes an epidemic that ultimately affected tens of thousands of Americans from early 1930, with a second, smaller wave in 1931. It reconstructs how the adulterated extract was made and sold and how the cause was traced. The article is the standard historical account of the epidemic.

citation: Petroianu GA. Neuropathic organophosphates: from Scrugham, Heim and Lorot to Jake leg paralysis. Die Pharmazie 71(6). 2016.
summary: Petroianu traced the history of the neuropathic organophosphates from their nineteenth-century chemistry to the Jamaica ginger paralysis of 1930. The nerve damage these compounds cause had been recognised in France before the epidemic, and the adulterant in the extract was identified soon after it. The paper places the jake leg epidemic in the longer history of toxic chemistry.

citation: Jennifer Billing. Antimicrobial Functions of Spices: Why Some Like it Hot. The Quarterly Review of Biology. 1998.
summary: Billing and colleagues counted the use of 43 spices in thousands of meat-based recipes from 36 countries and related it to climate. Spice use rose with mean temperature, and the most-used spices were those with the strongest antimicrobial activity in laboratory tests. They argued that spice use helped protect against food-borne pathogens, an argument still debated.

citation: Paul W. Sherman. Darwinian Gastronomy: Why We Use Spices. BioScience. 1999.
summary: Sherman and colleagues set out for a general readership the argument that spice use is an adaptation against food-borne microbes, drawing on the cross-cultural recipe analysis published the year before. They reviewed the evidence that the most-used spices are the most antimicrobial and that use rises in hot climates. The hypothesis remains debated, with flavour and cultural explanations offered as alternatives.

citation: Spence C. Ginger: The pungent spice. International Journal of Gastronomy and Food Science. 2023.
summary: A review of ginger's place in food and flavour, including its decline in British cooking after the seventeenth century and the perception of its pungency.

citation: Mowrey DB, Clayson DE. MOTION SICKNESS, GINGER, AND PSYCHOPHYSICS. The Lancet. 1982.
summary: Mowrey and Clayson compared powdered ginger, dimenhydrinate and placebo in students highly susceptible to motion sickness, who sat in a motorised rotating chair. A later tabulation reports that the ginger group stayed in the chair longest. The full paper was not read for this guide, and the result is taken from that secondary source.
why_it_mattered: It was the first controlled study of ginger for motion sickness, published in The Lancet, and it launched the modern research on ginger as an antiemetic.
read_note: PubMed record (no abstract) and secondary tabulation (BestBETs); full text not read

citation: BestBETs (Manchester Royal Infirmary). The use of ginger in the prevention of motion sickness (BestBET). bestbets.org. 2011.
summary: A BestBETs evidence summary from Manchester Royal Infirmary tabulating the trials of ginger for preventing motion sickness.

citation: Grøntved A, Brask T, Kambskard J, Hentzer E. Ginger root against seasickness. A controlled trial on the open sea. Acta Oto-Laryngologica 105(1-2):45-49. 1988.
summary: Grøntved and colleagues gave 1 g of powdered ginger or placebo to 80 naval cadets unaccustomed to heavy seas, double-blind. Ginger reduced vomiting and cold sweating significantly, while its effects on nausea and vertigo did not reach significance. It is the main trial of ginger under real seagoing conditions.
why_it_mattered: It is the classic field trial of ginger at sea and supports its regulatory acceptance for motion sickness.

citation: Wood CD, Manno JE, Wood MJ, Manno BR, Mims ME. Comparison of efficacy of ginger with various antimotion sickness drugs. Clinical Research Practices and Drug Regulatory Affairs 6(2):129-136 (NASA NTRS 20040090211). 1988.
summary: Wood and colleagues, with NASA support, compared three doses of ginger with standard antimotion-sickness drugs in laboratory motion tests. Ginger performed no better than placebo, whereas dimenhydrinate, promethazine and scopolamine gave protection. It is one of the principal negative laboratory studies.
why_it_mattered: It is the most cited negative laboratory test of ginger for motion sickness and frames the conflict in the evidence.

citation: Stewart JJ, Wood MJ, Wood CD, Mims ME. Effects of ginger on motion sickness susceptibility and gastric function. Pharmacology 42(2):111-120. 1991.
summary: Stewart and colleagues tested powdered and fresh ginger in 28 volunteers in a rotating-chair model of motion sickness and measured gastric function. Neither form of ginger gave any protection, and powdered ginger did not change gastric emptying. The study adds to the negative laboratory evidence.
why_it_mattered: It tested both fresh and powdered ginger and found neither effective, weakening the early positive result.

citation: Holtmann S et al. The Anti-motion Sickness Mechanism of Ginger: A Comparative Study with Placebo and Dimenhydrinate. Acta Oto-Laryngologica. 1989.
summary: Holtmann and colleagues recorded eye movements (nystagmus) under vestibular and visual stimulation after ginger, placebo and dimenhydrinate. Ginger did not differ from placebo, whereas dimenhydrinate damped the responses. The authors concluded that ginger does not act on the balance system and that any benefit more likely arises in the gut.
why_it_mattered: It is the classic study showing that ginger does not work like conventional motion-sickness drugs on the balance system.

citation: Han‐Chung Lien. Effects of ginger on motion sickness and gastric slow-wave dysrhythmias induced by circular vection. American Journal of Physiology-Gastrointestinal and Liver Physiology. 2003.
summary: Lien and colleagues induced motion sickness in 13 volunteers with a rotating visual drum and recorded the electrical rhythm of the stomach. Ginger reduced nausea and the abnormal gastric rhythms that accompanied it. The study supports a gastric site of action.

citation: Chrubasik S. Zingiberis rhizoma: a comprehensive review on the ginger effect and efficacy profiles. Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology. 2005.
summary: Chrubasik and colleagues reviewed the pharmacological and clinical literature on ginger to the early 2000s. They found some evidence for antiemetic effects and little or inconsistent evidence for most other indications, and noted the variable quality and composition of the preparations studied. The review is a sceptical benchmark for the early clinical literature.
why_it_mattered: It was the first comprehensive critical review of the clinical evidence and set the cautious frame that later systematic reviews refined.

citation: Fischer-Rasmussen W et al. Ginger treatment of hyperemesis gravidarum. European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology. 1991.
summary: Fischer-Rasmussen and colleagues ran the first randomised trial of ginger in pregnancy, a double-blind crossover in 30 women admitted with hyperemesis gravidarum, of whom 27 completed. Each woman took powdered ginger and placebo for four days each; most preferred the ginger period, and relief scores were significantly better with ginger. It opened the clinical study of ginger in pregnancy.
why_it_mattered: It was the first randomised trial of ginger in pregnancy and the starting point of the pregnancy evidence.

citation: Vutyavanich T. Ginger for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy: randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2001.
summary: Vutyavanich and colleagues randomised 70 women with nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, at or before 17 weeks, to oral ginger 1 g a day or placebo for four days, double-masked. Ginger reduced nausea scores and vomiting episodes, and no adverse effect on pregnancy outcome was found. It is one of the most cited trials in the field.
why_it_mattered: It is the best-known placebo-controlled trial of ginger in ordinary pregnancy sickness and anchors most later meta-analyses.

citation: Willetts KE et al. Effect of a ginger extract on pregnancy‐induced nausea: A randomised controlled trial. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 2003.
summary: Willetts and colleagues randomised 120 women less than 20 weeks pregnant to a standardised ginger extract or placebo four times a day for four days. Nausea fell from the first day, retching less so, and there was no significant effect on vomiting. Follow-up found normal birthweights, gestational ages and malformation rates.
why_it_mattered: It tested a standardised extract and reported birth outcomes, adding safety data to the efficacy evidence.

citation: Smith C et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial of Ginger to Treat Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2004.
summary: Smith and colleagues randomised 291 women less than 16 weeks pregnant to ginger or vitamin B6 daily for three weeks in an equivalence trial. Ginger and vitamin B6 reduced nausea, retching and vomiting to an equivalent extent. It is the largest early trial comparing ginger with an active treatment in pregnancy.
why_it_mattered: It established ginger as roughly equivalent to vitamin B6, a common first-line treatment, in the largest early pregnancy trial.

citation: Borrelli F et al. Effectiveness and Safety of Ginger in the Treatment of Pregnancy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2005.
summary: Borrelli and colleagues systematically reviewed six double-blind randomised trials of ginger for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, with 675 women in total. Four trials favoured ginger over placebo and two found it about as effective as vitamin B6; no adverse effect on pregnancy outcome was reported in the trials. The authors called for larger studies to confirm safety.
why_it_mattered: It was the first systematic review of ginger in pregnancy nausea and is cited by nearly every later review and guideline on the subject.

citation: Estelle Viljoen. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect and safety of ginger in the treatment of pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting. Nutrition Journal. 2014.
summary: Viljoen and colleagues systematically reviewed and meta-analysed trials of ginger for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, including safety outcomes. Ginger improved nausea compared with placebo but did not significantly reduce vomiting episodes. No significant increase in miscarriage or other harms was found, though the confidence interval for miscarriage was too wide to exclude one.

citation: Kendra A. Tiani. The Use of Ginger Bioactive Compounds in Pregnancy: An Evidence Scan and Umbrella Review of Existing Meta-Analyses. Advances in Nutrition. 2024.
summary: An evidence scan and umbrella review of ginger in pregnancy and lactation, appraising seven meta-analyses of pregnancy nausea and finding the evidence on safety and on uses other than nausea thin.

citation: Matthews A et al. Interventions for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015.
summary: The Cochrane review of interventions for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, updated in 2015, included 41 trials with 5449 women covering many treatments, among them ginger. Two reviewers in pairs assessed each trial's risk of bias. The review found the evidence for ginger and most other treatments limited and inconsistent.

citation: Bone ME et al. Ginger root—a new antiemetic The effect of ginger root on postoperative nausea and vomiting after major gynaecological surgery. Anaesthesia. 1990.
summary: Bone and colleagues compared ginger root, metoclopramide and placebo in 60 women having major gynaecological surgery, in a double-blind randomised trial. Fewer episodes of nausea were recorded with ginger than with placebo, and ginger performed about as well as metoclopramide. The trial was small and later trials gave mixed results.
why_it_mattered: It was among the first randomised trials of ginger for postoperative nausea, and its positive result prompted the trials and meta-analyses that followed.

citation: Arfeen Z et al. A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial of Ginger for the Prevention of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting. Anaesthesia and Intensive Care. 1995.
summary: Arfeen and colleagues randomised 108 women having gynaecological laparoscopy to placebo or 0.5 g or 1.0 g of ginger before anaesthesia, double-blind. Ginger did not reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting, and the higher dose tended to do worse. The trial is a well-known negative result in the postoperative literature.
why_it_mattered: It is the best-known negative trial of ginger for postoperative nausea and shows why the pooled evidence is mixed.

citation: Ernst E, Pittler MH. Efficacy of ginger for nausea and vomiting: a systematic review of randomized clinical trials. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2000.
summary: Ernst and Pittler made the first systematic review of randomised trials of ginger for nausea and vomiting of any cause, including six studies. The pooled reduction in postoperative nausea was not significant, while single trials in seasickness, morning sickness and chemotherapy nausea were positive. They concluded that ginger was a promising antiemetic but that the evidence was too thin to be sure.
why_it_mattered: It was the first systematic review of ginger as an antiemetic and set the agenda for the trials that followed.

citation: Nathorn Chaiyakunapruk. The efficacy of ginger for the prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting: A meta-analysis. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2006.
summary: Chaiyakunapruk and colleagues meta-analysed five randomised trials, 363 patients in total, of a fixed dose of at least 1 g of ginger against placebo before surgery. Ginger reduced the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting over 24 hours. The authors noted the small number of trials and their varying quality.

citation: Kalava A et al. Efficacy of ginger on intraoperative and postoperative nausea and vomiting in elective cesarean section patients. European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology. 2013.
summary: Kalava and colleagues randomised 239 women having elective caesarean section under combined spinal–epidural anaesthesia to oral dried ginger or placebo before surgery. Ginger did not reduce nausea or vomiting during or after the operation. It is one of the larger negative trials in the perioperative setting.

citation: Pillai AK et al. Anti‐emetic effect of ginger powder versus placebo as an add‐on therapy in children and young adults receiving high emetogenic chemotherapy. Pediatric Blood & Cancer. 2010.
summary: Pillai and colleagues randomised sixty cycles of cisplatin and doxorubicin chemotherapy in children and young adults with bone sarcoma to ginger root powder or placebo, added to ondansetron and dexamethasone. Moderate to severe acute and delayed nausea and vomiting were all significantly less frequent with ginger. It is one of the few trials of ginger in younger patients, and it is small.

citation: Ryan JL. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) reduces acute chemotherapy-induced nausea: a URCC CCOP study of 576 patients. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2012.
summary: Ryan and colleagues randomised 744 cancer patients in a multicentre double-blind trial to placebo or 0.5 g, 1.0 g or 1.5 g of ginger a day, added to standard antiemetics; 576 were analysed. All ginger doses reduced acute nausea on the first day of chemotherapy, the lower doses most. It is the largest trial of ginger for chemotherapy nausea.
why_it_mattered: It is the largest trial of ginger in chemotherapy-induced nausea and the main positive result in that indication.

citation: Zick SM et al. Phase II trial of encapsulated ginger as a treatment for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2008.
summary: Zick and colleagues randomised 162 adults receiving chemotherapy, already on standard antiemetics, to 1 g or 2 g of ginger a day or placebo for three days. Ginger made no difference to delayed nausea and vomiting, or to any secondary measure. It is the main negative trial in the chemotherapy indication.
why_it_mattered: It is the best-known negative trial of ginger for chemotherapy nausea and keeps the pooled evidence mixed.

citation: Megan Crichton. Effect of a Standardized Ginger Root Powder Regimen on Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting: A Multicenter, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 2023.
summary: A two-centre double-blind trial of a standardised ginger root powder against placebo, added to antiemetics during chemotherapy in 103 adults, with mixed effects on nausea and quality of life.

citation: Marx W et al. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: a systematic literature review. Nutrition Reviews. 2013.
summary: Marx and colleagues systematically reviewed seven studies of ginger as the only variable tested against chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Three showed a benefit, two favoured ginger with caveats and two showed no effect. They identified methodological limitations and called for better trials before clinical use can be recommended.

citation: Jihee Choi. Effects of Ginger Intake on Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting: A Systematic Review of Randomized Clinical Trials. Nutrients. 2022.
summary: A systematic review and subgroup meta-analysis of randomised trials of ginger for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, with effects varying by outcome and chemotherapy type.

citation: Nguyễn Hoàng Anh. Ginger on Human Health: A Comprehensive Systematic Review of 109 Randomized Controlled Trials. Nutrients. 2020.
summary: Anh and colleagues systematically reviewed 109 randomised controlled trials of ginger in humans across every indication reported. They found the most consistent evidence for nausea and vomiting, some for anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, and few serious adverse events. The review maps how widely ginger has been tested and how uneven the quality of the trials is.

citation: Bliddal H et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled, cross-over study of ginger extracts and Ibuprofen in osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis and Cartilage. 2000.
summary: Bliddal and colleagues compared a ginger extract, ibuprofen and placebo for three weeks each in a crossover trial in people with osteoarthritis of the hip or knee. In the first period ibuprofen did better than ginger on some measures, and in the crossover analysis ginger did not differ clearly from placebo. The study is an early, largely negative test of ginger for joint pain.
why_it_mattered: It was one of the first controlled trials of a ginger extract in osteoarthritis and tempered early claims for joint pain.

citation: Roy Davis Altman. Effects of a ginger extract on knee pain in patients with osteoarthritis. Arthritis & Rheumatism. 2001.
summary: Altman and colleagues ran a six-week multicentre double-blind trial of a concentrated extract of two ginger-family species in 261 people with knee osteoarthritis. More people on the extract than on placebo had a meaningful reduction in knee pain on standing, with more mild stomach complaints. The extract contained galangal as well as ginger, so the result is not for ginger alone.
why_it_mattered: It is the largest early trial of a ginger-containing extract in osteoarthritis and is cited in most reviews of the indication.

citation: Bartels EM et al. Efficacy and safety of ginger in osteoarthritis patients: a meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials. Osteoarthritis and Cartilage. 2014.
summary: Bartels and colleagues meta-analysed five randomised placebo-controlled trials, with 593 patients, of oral ginger in osteoarthritis. Ginger produced a small, statistically significant reduction in pain and in disability, and patients on ginger were more than twice as likely to stop treatment. The authors called ginger modestly efficacious and reasonably safe.

citation: Terry R et al. The Use of Ginger ( Zingiber officinale ) for the Treatment of Pain: A Systematic Review of Clinical Trials. Pain Medicine. 2011.
summary: Terry and colleagues systematically reviewed eight trials, with 481 participants, of ginger as the sole oral treatment for pain. Six trials, in osteoarthritis, period pain and experimentally induced muscle pain, found that ginger reduced reported pain, but the methodological quality was variable. The authors judged the evidence insufficient while giving tentative support to an anti-inflammatory role.

citation: Black CD et al. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) Reduces Muscle Pain Caused by Eccentric Exercise. Journal of Pain. 2010.
summary: Black and colleagues ran two identical placebo-controlled trials in which volunteers took 2 g of raw or of heat-treated ginger a day for 11 days and then did eccentric exercise to induce muscle pain. Both forms reduced pain the day after exercise by a similar amount compared with placebo, and heat treatment did not enhance the effect. It is one of the few comparisons of raw and heated ginger.

citation: Ozgoli G et al. Comparison of Effects of Ginger, Mefenamic Acid, and Ibuprofen on Pain in Women with Primary Dysmenorrhea. The Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine. 2009.
summary: Ozgoli and colleagues allocated 150 students with primary dysmenorrhoea to ginger powder, mefenamic acid or ibuprofen for three days from the start of menstruation, double-blind. Pain relief and satisfaction did not differ between the three groups. It is the classic trial comparing ginger with standard painkillers for period pain.
why_it_mattered: It is the first trial to show ginger performing on a par with standard drugs for period pain and is cited in every later review.

citation: James William Daily. Efficacy of Ginger for Alleviating the Symptoms of Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. Pain Medicine. 2015.
summary: Daily and colleagues systematically reviewed ginger for primary dysmenorrhoea and pooled four placebo-controlled trials. Ginger reduced pain scores compared with placebo, but the trials were few and small and their quality was limited. The authors judged the evidence suggestive rather than conclusive.

citation: Reza Moshfeghinia. Ginger for Pain Management in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Integrative and Complementary Medicine. 2024.
summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies of ginger for pain in primary dysmenorrhoea, finding benefit over placebo with high heterogeneity and no difference from anti-inflammatory drugs.

citation: Laís Bhering Martins. Double-blind placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial of ginger ( Zingiber officinale Rosc. ) addition in migraine acute treatment. Cephalalgia. 2018.
summary: Martins and colleagues randomised 60 adults with migraine to a ginger extract or placebo, each added to the anti-inflammatory drug ketoprofen for acute attacks. The ginger group had better pain relief at one and two hours and more people pain-free, with no more side effects. It is a small single trial.

citation: Jie Zhu. Effects of Ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe) on Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Components of the Metabolic Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Evidence-based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2018.
summary: Zhu and colleagues meta-analysed ten randomised trials, with 490 people, of ginger in type 2 diabetes and the metabolic syndrome. Ginger lowered blood glucose and HbA1c and improved some lipid measures, though not all. The trials were small and short, and the authors called for better studies.

citation: Armin Ebrahimzadeh. The effect of ginger supplementation on metabolic profiles in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Complementary Therapies in Medicine. 2022.
summary: A meta-analysis of ten trials of ginger supplementation in type 2 diabetes, reporting reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c and some lipids and blood-pressure measures.

citation: Bordia A et al. Effect of ginger (Zingiber officinale Rosc.) and fenugreek (Trigonella foenumgraecum L.) on blood lipids, blood sugar and platelet aggregation in patients with coronary artery disease. Prostaglandins Leukotrienes and Essential Fatty Acids. 1997.
summary: Bordia and colleagues gave ginger or fenugreek to healthy people, people with coronary artery disease and people with type 2 diabetes in a placebo-controlled study, and measured blood lipids, sugar and platelet aggregation. Three months of powdered ginger did not change platelet aggregation, whereas a single large dose reduced it in people with coronary disease. The study is the main human source for the question of ginger and bleeding risk.
why_it_mattered: It is the human study most cited on whether ginger affects platelets, and it separates the effects of usual and very large doses.

citation: Shrin Rjabi. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of ginger supplementation in adults: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose–response meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Inflammopharmacology. 2025.
summary: A GRADE-assessed dose–response meta-analysis of 29 trials of ginger on inflammatory and antioxidant biomarkers in adults, finding reductions in C-reactive protein and other markers at low to moderate certainty.

citation: Vali Musazadeh. Ginger supplementation and metabolic health: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomized trials. Diabetology & Metabolic Syndrome. 2026.
summary: An umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomised trials of ginger on metabolic and inflammatory measures, grading the credibility of each pooled result.

citation: Keshab Raj Paudel. Pharmacological properties of ginger (Zingiber officinale): what do meta-analyses say? a systematic review. Frontiers in Pharmacology. 2025.
summary: A systematic review of meta-analyses published from 2010 to 2025 on ginger and inflammation, type 2 diabetes, oxidative stress and pregnancy nausea.

citation: Portnoi G et al. Prospective comparative study of the safety and effectiveness of ginger for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2003.
summary: Portnoi and colleagues followed women who called the Motherisk Program in Toronto while taking ginger in the first trimester, and compared them with women exposed to non-teratogenic drugs. Of 187 pregnancies with known outcome, malformation rates and other outcomes did not differ from the comparison group. It is the first prospective cohort study of ginger safety in pregnancy.
why_it_mattered: It was the first prospective safety cohort of ginger in pregnancy and is cited in regulatory and clinical guidance.

citation: Srivastava KC. Effect of onion and ginger consumption on platelet thromboxane production in humans. Prostaglandins Leukotrienes and Essential Fatty Acids. 1989.
summary: Srivastava had healthy Danish women eat 70 g of raw onion or 5 g of raw ginger a day for a week and measured thromboxane, a platelet-activating compound, in serum. Thromboxane fell in the ginger group, which was small. The study was the first sign in people that ginger might affect platelets.
why_it_mattered: It is the human study behind early warnings that ginger might increase bleeding, later tested with dried ginger.

citation: Effie Nurtjahja-Tjendraputra. Effective anti-platelet and COX-1 enzyme inhibitors from pungent constituents of ginger. Thrombosis Research. 2003.
summary: Nurtjahja-Tjendraputra and colleagues tested 20 pungent constituents of ginger and related compounds on human platelets in vitro. Several inhibited arachidonic acid-induced platelet activation and the COX-1 enzyme, some more potently than aspirin. The study identifies which compounds could, in principle, affect clotting.

citation: Lumb AB. Effect of Dried Ginger on Human Platelet Function. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 1994.
summary: Lumb gave eight healthy men 2 g of dried ginger or placebo in a randomised double-blind study and measured bleeding time and platelet function over 24 hours. Ginger had no effect on any measure. The author concluded that ordinary doses of dried ginger are unlikely to impair platelets.
why_it_mattered: It is the key controlled study showing that a usual dose of dried ginger does not affect platelet function.

citation: Xuemin Jiang. Effect of ginkgo and ginger on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of warfarin in healthy subjects. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2005.
summary: Jiang and colleagues gave 12 healthy men a single dose of warfarin alone or after a week of ginkgo or ginger, in an open three-way crossover. Ginger did not change warfarin's levels or its effect on clotting, nor did it affect platelet aggregation on its own. The study is the main direct test of a ginger–warfarin interaction.
why_it_mattered: It is the principal direct test of whether ginger interacts with warfarin and found no interaction.

citation: Shalansky S et al. Risk of Warfarin‐Related Bleeding Events and Supratherapeutic International Normalized Ratios Associated with Complementary and Alternative Medicine: A Longitudinal Analysis. Pharmacotherapy The Journal of Human Pharmacology and Drug Therapy. 2007.
summary: Shalansky and colleagues followed 171 adults on warfarin for 16 weeks with diaries of bleeding events and use of complementary medicines. Ginger was among the products associated with self-reported bleeding. As an observational study it cannot show cause, but it is the main signal of risk in patients.
why_it_mattered: It is the main signal from patients that ginger use may be associated with bleeding on warfarin.

citation: Leon PJ Vaes. Interactions of Warfarin with Garlic, Ginger, Ginkgo, or Ginseng: Nature of the Evidence. Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2000.
summary: Vaes and colleagues reviewed the evidence to 1999 for interactions of warfarin with garlic, ginger, ginkgo and ginseng. For ginger they found only theoretical or in vitro grounds and no well-documented clinical case. The review shows how thin the early basis for interaction warnings was.

citation: Grzanna R et al. Ginger—An Herbal Medicinal Product with Broad Anti-Inflammatory Actions. Journal of Medicinal Food. 2005.
summary: Grzanna and colleagues reviewed the anti-inflammatory pharmacology of ginger. Its inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis, first described in the 1970s, was extended to the leukotriene pathway through 5-lipoxygenase, a combination unlike ordinary anti-inflammatory drugs. The review summarises the laboratory basis for ginger's use in inflammatory conditions.
why_it_mattered: It is the standard review of ginger's dual action on the prostaglandin and leukotriene pathways.

citation: Kiuchi F et al. Inhibition of Prostaglandin and Leukotriene Biosynthesis by Gingerols and Diarylheptanoids. Chemical and Pharmaceutical Bulletin. 1992.
summary: Kiuchi and colleagues identified gingerols and diarylheptanoids from ginger and a related plant as inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis. Predicting from their structures that they would also block 5-lipoxygenase, they confirmed it experimentally. The paper identified the compounds behind ginger's anti-inflammatory activity in the laboratory.
why_it_mattered: It identified the specific ginger compounds that inhibit both prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis.

citation: Abdel-Aziz H et al. Mode of action of gingerols and shogaols on 5-HT3 receptors: Binding studies, cation uptake by the receptor channel and contraction of isolated guinea-pig ileum. European Journal of Pharmacology. 2006.
summary: Abdel-Aziz and colleagues tested how gingerols and 6-shogaol act on the 5-HT3 receptor, the serotonin receptor targeted by modern antiemetic drugs. Using binding studies, cation uptake and isolated tissue, they found the compounds blocked the receptor without competing at its serotonin site. The work offers one plausible mechanism for ginger's effect on nausea.
why_it_mattered: It gave the first detailed account of how ginger compounds interact with the 5-HT3 receptor, the leading mechanistic explanation for an antiemetic effect.

citation: Jutta Walstab. Ginger and its pungent constituents non‐competitively inhibit activation of human recombinant and native 5‐HT3 receptors of enteric neurons. Neurogastroenterology & Motility. 2013.
summary: Walstab and colleagues tested ginger extracts and constituents on human 5-HT3 receptors in cells and in human gut tissue. The compounds inhibited the receptor non-competitively, as earlier rodent studies had suggested. The study carried the 5-HT3 mechanism from animals to human receptors.

citation: Heinz H. Pertz. Effects of Ginger Constituents on the Gastrointestinal Tract: Role of Cholinergic M3and Serotonergic 5-HT3and 5-HT4Receptors. Planta Medica. 2011.
summary: Pertz and colleagues tested gingerols and 6-shogaol on isolated tissue at three receptors involved in nausea and gut movement, M3, 5-HT3 and 5-HT4. The compounds acted on several of these receptors, and their effects differed with chain length. The study suggests that ginger acts on more than one target in the gut.

citation: Yamahara J et al. Gastrointestinal motility enhancing effect of ginger and its active constituents. Chemical and Pharmaceutical Bulletin. 1990.
summary: Yamahara and colleagues tested ginger extract and its constituents on the movement of a charcoal meal through the gut of mice. The extract, 6-shogaol and the gingerols all speeded transit, with effects similar to or slightly weaker than the drugs metoclopramide and domperidone. The study is the classic animal evidence that ginger promotes gut motility.
why_it_mattered: It is the classic animal demonstration that ginger compounds speed gut transit, the basis for the gastric explanation of ginger's effects.

citation: Keng‐Liang Wu. Effects of ginger on gastric emptying and motility in healthy humans. European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2008.
summary: Wu and colleagues gave 24 healthy volunteers ginger or placebo in a randomised double-blind crossover and measured stomach emptying and movement. Ginger speeded gastric emptying and increased contractions of the lower stomach, without changing symptoms. The study supports a gastric mechanism in people.

citation: Ming‐Luen Hu. Effect of ginger on gastric motility and symptoms of functional dyspepsia. World Journal of Gastroenterology. 2010.
summary: Hu and colleagues studied 11 patients with functional dyspepsia twice, after ginger and after placebo, in a randomised double-blind crossover. Ginger speeded gastric emptying and stimulated the lower stomach, but did not change symptoms or gut hormones. The study shows a measurable effect on the stomach without a clear symptomatic benefit.

citation: Dedov VN et al. Gingerols: a novel class of vanilloid receptor (VR1) agonists. British Journal of Pharmacology. 2002.
summary: Dedov and colleagues synthesised 6- and 8-gingerol and tested them on cultured sensory neurons. Both behaved like capsaicin, activating the vanilloid receptor VR1 (TRPV1), and the effect was blocked by the antagonist capsazepine. The study identified the receptor responsible for ginger's heat.
why_it_mattered: It established gingerols as TRPV1 agonists, the molecular explanation for why ginger tastes hot.

citation: Yusaku Iwasaki. A nonpungent component of steamed ginger - [10]-shogaol - increases adrenaline secretion via the activation of TRPV1. Nutritional Neuroscience. 2006.
summary: Iwasaki and colleagues tested gingerols and shogaols for their ability to activate the TRPV1 receptor and raise adrenaline secretion and body temperature. All activated the receptor, and 10-shogaol, abundant in steamed ginger, did so while being much less pungent. The study shows that heat and pungency can be separated.

citation: Yue Yin. Structural mechanisms underlying activation of TRPV1 channels by pungent compounds in gingers. British Journal of Pharmacology. 2019.
summary: Yin and colleagues combined structural modelling, electrophysiology and mutation of the receptor to show how ginger's pungent compounds bind and open the TRPV1 channel. The compounds sit in the same pocket as capsaicin, with differences that explain their weaker potency. The study gives a structural basis for ginger's heat.

citation: Shuwei Zhang. Pharmacokinetics of Gingerols, Shogaols, and Their Metabolites in Asthma Patients. Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry. 2022.
summary: A pharmacokinetic study of gingerols, shogaols and their metabolites in people with asthma taking ginger extract for 56 days, which again found the compounds mainly as conjugates in blood.

citation: Rao Mukkavilli. Absorption, Metabolic Stability, and Pharmacokinetics of Ginger Phytochemicals. Molecules. 2017.
summary: Mukkavilli and colleagues measured the solubility, metabolic stability and absorption of the main ginger phenolics in vitro and in mice. The compounds were rapidly conjugated, but the whole extract gave better exposure than the isolated compounds. The study adds animal data to the human bioavailability problem.

citation: Mahady GB et al. Ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe) and the gingerols inhibit the growth of Cag A+ strains of Helicobacter pylori. PubMed. 2003.
summary: Mahady and colleagues tested a methanol extract of dried ginger and its gingerols and 6-shogaol against 19 strains of Helicobacter pylori, including CagA-positive strains, in vitro. The extract and the gingerols inhibited growth at low concentrations. The study is a laboratory result that has not been tested in people.
why_it_mattered: It is the most cited laboratory evidence for ginger against Helicobacter pylori, the bacterium linked to ulcers.

citation: Ali BH et al. Some phytochemical, pharmacological and toxicological properties of ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe): A review of recent research. Food and Chemical Toxicology. 2007.
summary: Ali and colleagues reviewed the chemistry, pharmacology and toxicology of ginger, drawing on animal, cell and human studies. They summarised ginger's long use in Chinese, Ayurvedic and Unani medicine and reported generally low toxicity in animal studies. The review is widely cited as a broad reference but relies heavily on preclinical work.
why_it_mattered: It is one of the most cited general reviews of ginger's pharmacology and toxicology.

citation: Denniff P, Whiting DA. Biosynthesis of [6]-gingerol, pungent principle of Zingiber officinale. Journal of the Chemical Society Chemical Communications. 1976.
summary: Denniff and Whiting fed labelled precursors to ginger and traced them into 6-gingerol. They proposed that phenylalanine is built up to a phenylpropanoid unit that condenses with malonate and hexanoate, and that the resulting diketone is reduced to gingerol. The paper is the first experimental outline of how ginger makes its pungent compounds.
why_it_mattered: It proposed the biosynthetic route to gingerols that genome and enzyme studies have been testing ever since.

citation: Denniff P, Macleod I, Whiting DA. Studies in the biosynthesis of [6]-gingerol, pungent principle of ginger (Zingiber officinale). Journal of the Chemical Society Perkin Transactions 1. 1980.
summary: Denniff, Macleod and Whiting extended their feeding experiments to whole plants and rhizome sections. The labelling showed phenylalanine converted to ferulic acid, which condenses with malonate and hexanoate in an unusual Claisen-type reaction before reduction to 6-gingerol. The full paper confirmed and detailed the 1976 proposal.
why_it_mattered: It is the full experimental account of gingerol biosynthesis, and its predicted condensation step was finally matched to an enzyme in 2026.

citation: Maria del Carmen Ramirez-Ahumada. Biosynthesis of curcuminoids and gingerols in turmeric (Curcuma longa) and ginger (Zingiber officinale): Identification of curcuminoid synthase and hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA thioesterases. Phytochemistry. 2006.
summary: Ramirez-Ahumada and colleagues assayed the enzymes of the phenylpropanoid pathway in leaf, shoot and rhizome extracts of ginger and turmeric. The pathway enzymes were active in both plants, but in ginger a thioesterase destroyed the feruloyl-CoA precursor in the test tube and masked any gingerol-forming activity. The study explained why the key ginger enzyme was so hard to find.
why_it_mattered: It mapped the early pathway enzymes in ginger and showed why direct detection of gingerol synthesis failed, a problem solved only in 2026.

citation: Hyun Jo Koo. Ginger and turmeric expressed sequence tags identify signature genes for rhizome identity and development and the biosynthesis of curcuminoids, gingerols and terpenoids. BMC Plant Biology 13:27. 2013.
summary: Koo and colleagues sequenced expressed genes from eight tissues of ginger and turmeric and identified genes specific to rhizome identity and development. They proposed pathways for gingerol and curcuminoid biosynthesis from the gene data. The study was an early genomic resource for both plants.

citation: Yusong Jiang. Transcriptome Analysis Provides Insights into Gingerol Biosynthesis in Ginger ( Zingiber officinale ). The Plant Genome. 2018.
summary: Jiang and colleagues sequenced the transcriptome of ginger tissues and rhizome stages and measured gingerol content in each. Genes for the proposed gingerol pathway were most active where gingerols accumulated. The study refined the candidate gene list for gingerol biosynthesis.

citation: Christine Ficker. Bioassay‐guided isolation and identiﬁcation of antifungal compounds from ginger. Phytotherapy Research. 2003.
summary: Ficker and colleagues fractionated an extract of an African land race of ginger, guided by antifungal tests. The main antifungal compounds were 6-, 8- and 10-gingerol and 6-gingerdiol, active against a range of human pathogenic fungi. The study links ginger's pungent compounds to defence against fungi.

citation: Muhammad Talib Kalhoro. Fungicidal properties of ginger (Zingiber officinale) essential oils against Phytophthora colocasiae. Scientific Reports. 2022.
summary: An in vitro test of ginger essential oil against Phytophthora colocasiae, the cause of taro leaf blight, which found that the oil inhibited the pathogen.

citation: Lingling Zhang. Antibacterial activity and mechanism of ginger extract against Ralstonia solanacearum. Journal of Applied Microbiology. 2022.
summary: Chemical profiling of a ginger extract and tests of its activity against Ralstonia solanacearum, the cause of bacterial wilt, with evidence that it damages the bacterial cell membrane.

citation: Keke Dang. Root Exudates of Ginger Induced by Ralstonia solanacearum Infection Could Inhibit Bacterial Wilt. Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry. 2023.
summary: A study of how ginger's root exudates and root bacteria change during Ralstonia solanacearum infection, finding exudate compounds that inhibited the pathogen.

citation: Duy Phu Le. Pythium soft rot of ginger: Detection and identification of the causal pathogens, and their control. Crop Protection. 2014.
summary: Le and colleagues reviewed Pythium soft rot of ginger, one of the most damaging diseases of the crop. They covered the species of Pythium responsible, methods of detecting and identifying them, and control measures including clean planting material. The review is a standard reference for growers and plant pathologists.

citation: Wenbo Wang. Metabolome-driven microbiome assembly determining the health of ginger crop (Zingiber officinale L. Roscoe) against rhizome rot. Microbiome. 2024.
summary: A microbiome and metabolome comparison of healthy ginger plants and plants with rhizome rot, showing that the plant's metabolites shape the microbial community around it.

citation: B. Jasim. Isolation and characterization of plant growth promoting endophytic bacteria from the rhizome of Zingiber officinale. 3 Biotech. 2013.
summary: Jasim and colleagues isolated bacteria living inside ginger rhizome and characterised those that promoted plant growth. Several endophytes produced plant hormones and other growth-promoting factors. The study shows that the rhizome carries a community of beneficial microbes.

citation: Kavitha PG, Thomas G. Defence transcriptome profiling of Zingiber zerumbet (L.) Smith by mRNA differential display. Journal of Biosciences. 2008.
summary: Kavitha and Thomas used mRNA differential display to compare gene expression in a soft-rot-resistant accession of Zingiber zerumbet, a wild relative of ginger, challenged with Pythium. The largest group of induced genes was linked to defence, stress and signalling. The study points to resistance genes that cultivated ginger may lack.
why_it_mattered: It identified defence genes in a resistant wild relative, a starting point for breeding soft-rot resistance into ginger.

citation: Shangjia Liu. Effects of soil waterlogging and high-temperature stress on photosynthesis and photosystem II of ginger (Zingiber officinale). PROTOPLASMA. 2022.
summary: A controlled experiment showing that soil waterlogging and high temperature, alone and together, reduce photosynthesis and damage photosystem II in ginger.

citation: TO CONFIRM (authors include Zhiduan Chen, Rujie Shi, Hong-Lei Li). High-temperature and intense-light stress in ginger (title to confirm). Metabolites 13(9):992. 2023.
summary: A study of how combined high temperature and intense light affect ginger's growth and stress responses; the bibliographic details are still to be confirmed.

citation: Xue Lv. Comprehensive insights into the influence of supplemental green light on the photosynthesis of ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe). Protoplasma. 2022.
summary: An experiment showing that supplementing the green band of sunlight increased the photosynthesis of ginger.

citation: Yun Ren. Dynamic transcriptome profiling provides insights into rhizome enlargement in ginger (Zingiber officinale Rosc.). PLoS ONE. 2023.
summary: Hormone and transcriptome profiling of ginger rhizome at three stages of enlargement, identifying hormones and genes associated with rhizome swelling.

citation: A. R. Rafie, Teresa Olczyk, Waldo R. Guerrero. Hydroponic production of fresh ginger roots ( zingiber officinale ) as an alternative method for South Florida. Proceedings of the Florida State Horticultural Society. 2003.
summary: Rafie and Olczyk compared fresh ginger grown in a greenhouse hydroponic system in Florida with ginger grown in the field. The hydroponic system gave more yield and better-quality rhizomes, and preliminary observations suggested lower costs because of less disease, insect and weed control. It is an early practical test of growing ginger without soil under cover.

citation: Yaseer Suhaimi Mohd, Azizah Mohamad, S. Mahamud, D. Khadzir. Effects of organic substrates on growth and yield of ginger cultivated using soilless culture. Malaysian Applied Biology 44(3): 63–68. 2015.
summary: Suhaimi and colleagues grew ginger by fertigation under a rain shelter in Malaysia in five mixtures of coir dust and burnt paddy husk. Plants in 100% coir dust grew tallest and gave the highest rhizome yield, about twice that of the poorest mixture. The study supports cheap, locally available organic substrates for soilless ginger.

citation: Lurline Marsh, Fawzy Hashem, Brett D. Smith. Organic Ginger (Zingiber officinale Rosc.) Development in a Short Temperate Growing Season: Effect of Seedling Transplant Type and Mycorrhiza Application. American Journal of Plant Sciences. 2021.
summary: High-tunnel and field trials of organic ginger grown from seedling transplants in the short temperate growing season of the US Delmarva Peninsula.

citation: Minnesota Department of Agriculture. Ginger Wilt (Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum) fact sheet, June 2024. mda.state.mn.us/ginger-wilt. 2024.
summary: The Minnesota Department of Agriculture's fact sheet on ginger wilt, caused by Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum, after its detection in the state.

citation: Jung MY et al. Heat-induced conversion of gingerols to shogaols in ginger as affected by heat type (dry or moist heat), sample type (fresh or dried), temperature and time. Food Science and Biotechnology. 2017.
summary: Jung and colleagues used liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry to measure how heat type, sample type, temperature and time affect the conversion of gingerols to shogaols in ginger. Heat greatly increased the conversion, which rose with temperature, and moist heat was more effective than dry heat. The study gives the conditions that most change the chemistry of cooked ginger.

citation: Ali Ghasemzadeh. Formation of 6-, 8- and 10-Shogaol in Ginger through Application of Different Drying Methods: Altered Antioxidant and Antimicrobial Activity. Molecules. 2018.
summary: Ghasemzadeh and colleagues compared open sun drying, solar-tunnel drying and hot-air drying of ginger. All methods converted gingerols to 6-, 8- and 10-shogaol, the amounts depending on the method and temperature, and the dried ginger had higher antioxidant activity. The study links drying methods to the chemistry of the product.

citation: Master-Cooks of King Richard II; ed. Samuel Pegge. The Forme of Cury: A Roll of Ancient English Cookery, compiled about A.D. 1390. Project Gutenberg eBook #8102 (public domain in the USA). 1780.
summary: The Forme of Cury, a cookery roll compiled about 1390 by the master cooks of Richard II, in Samuel Pegge's 1780 edition; it includes the sauce gyngener.

It gives recipes for ginger beer and for several gingerbreads, including a 'plebeian' version made with molasses. The book is in the public domain and was read from a scan.

summary: Thomas Austin's 1888 edition of two fifteenth-century English cookery manuscripts for the Early English Text Society. It includes a recipe for gyngerbrede made of honey, breadcrumbs and spices but no ginger.

citation: Li H. Ginger for health care: An overview of systematic reviews. Complementary therapies in medicine. 2019.
summary: Li and colleagues summarised the evidence from 27 systematic reviews of ginger for any condition and appraised their quality. The strongest evidence was for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, with weaker or inconsistent evidence for other uses. Many of the reviews were of low methodological quality.
